text: State the business problem before the solution: what happens, what should happen, who is affected, what is unknown. The problem never names the fix.
Every statistic carries its source, population and evidence type. Forecasts and vendor surveys are labelled.
State the gap as 'the literature tells us X, but not Y', with one research-gap and one practitioner-gap sentence.
Never claim that nobody has studied the topic, and never use 'agents are new' as the gap. Treat close prior art as a rival.
Say the purpose in one breath with design, demonstrate and evaluate. Never 'explore'.
Each sub-problem maps to one objective (verb, number, deadline from t0) and one open, typed research question.
Each design proposition has a metric and a decision rule fixed before Cycle 1, and can fail.
Show SP → RO → RQ → DP → data → test with no empty cells.
Name the paradigm (pragmatism) and what it means for the evidence you accept.
Conceptual framework = kernel theory → requirement → design principle → feature, with the build–evaluate loop. The artefact has its own name.
Name DSRM and show its six activities, each with an output. Design is not method: name the data-collection methods inside it.
Plan evaluation with FEDS: artificial then naturalistic. A demonstration is not an evaluation.
For each participant group give role, count, inclusion and independence. Nothing is collected before IRB clearance.
Reject the alternatives (survey, case study, action research, PLS-SEM) in one sentence each.
Separate scope (your choices) from limitations (constraints); give each limitation a mitigation.
State two contributions: reusable design knowledge and the practical artefact. Do not claim results you do not have.
Show a leader using the framework on clearly labelled illustrative data: evidence, decision rule, action.
Be ready to defend every line, especially 'why this method, and do you really need it?'.
src: Course guidance (paraphrased); Researcher's Journey, DSR step 14
